segments.label: How overall improvement hides language-slice gaps
segments.summary: In this synthetic example, underlying fraud is equally common across languages. An English-centric description-quality score is lower for Hindi and Hinglish descriptions, and adding it improves overall fraud detection. The highest-scoring 10% of cases are flagged. Regional flag rates look nearly identical because languages are distributed evenly across regions. Language-specific detection tells a different story: the model detects 33.5% of fraud overall, but only about one-fifth of English-language fraud, over 40% of Hindi-language fraud, and more than half of Hinglish-language fraud. Overall improvement therefore coexists with uneven slice performance, including missed English-language fraud and burdens on innocent Hindi- and Hinglish-speaking customers.

remediation_steps.title: Revisit: the check — separate the slices

blocks.text: Contrast observed slice evidence with a population claim. Counts and sample conditioning support the former, not automatic generalization to the latter.

Overall improvement can coexist with uneven segment performance. For each predefined slice, report eligible count and errors/eligible count. Retain that conditioning population. Samples may not represent their intended population, so sample slice differences alone do not establish population-level disparity.

remediation_steps.title: Revisit: the check — check representation first

blocks.text: Contrast subgroup-conditional harm with population-weighted contribution. Weight by supplied deployment probability, then inspect representation and overall evidence too.

Check whether data represents intended groups before attributing a subgroup problem solely to the model. Evaluate the supplied mitigation on the affected validation segment and overall cohort. A subgroup’s contribution to total expected harm is its deployment population probability × subgroup-conditional expected harm, using supplied error costs.
FPR = FP/(FP+TN) conditions on actual negatives; FNR = FN/(FN+TP) conditions on actual positives. An empty conditioning group leaves its rate undefined.
